justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a mild upward drift across time horizons, starting near 217.5 for the one-day horizon and gradually rising to 220.0 at the one-month mark. The one-day estimate was anchored primarily to recent price action and short-term momentum, assuming no major overnight catalysts and a continuation of the prevailing trend. For the one-week and one-month estimates, I incorporated a slight positive bias reflecting the general tendency of the underlying asset to drift upward over time, consistent with longer-term trend assumptions. The incremental increases are modest because I did not have strong directional conviction — the estimates are closer to a "base case continuation" than a bold directional call.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which reflects the compounding nature of uncertainty over time. At one day, the interval is relatively tight at roughly plus or minus 5 points because intraday volatility is constrained and mean reversion forces tend to limit large single-session moves. By one week, realized volatility can accumulate across multiple sessions, and the interval expands to roughly plus or minus 10 points. At one month, macroeconomic data releases, earnings announcements, and shifting sentiment can all compound, widening the interval to plus or minus 20 points. The width ratios across horizons roughly follow a square-root-of-time scaling, which is a standard assumption under random walk dynamics.

There are several specific risks that could push outcomes well outside my stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected deterioration in macroeconomic data — such as a sharply negative jobs report, an escalation in geopolitical tensions, or a sudden tightening in financial conditions — could produce a move significantly below the lower bound of my one-month interval of 200. On the upside, a strong positive surprise such as a dovish central bank pivot, a breakthrough trade agreement, or a better-than-expected earnings season could push prices well above 240.

Additionally, tail risks that are difficult to model — such as a financial contagion event, a sudden liquidity crisis, or an unexpected geopolitical shock — are not fully captured in my intervals by construction. My confidence intervals represent a 90% coverage band, meaning roughly one in ten outcomes is expected to fall outside them under normal conditions, and fat-tailed distributions mean the actual frequency of extreme outcomes may be higher than that implied probability suggests. Anyone relying on these forecasts should treat the outer bounds as approximate guides rather than hard limits.
